title: AI in your community
essentialQuestion: How can AI help a community get its problems fixed, and who does the fixing?
learningGoal: Explain how Traffy Fondue in Thailand uses AI to sort and send residents' reports, why people and agencies still fix the problems, and what its numbers can and can't show.

evidence.question: Which steps does the AI do, and which steps do people do?

cards.title: How a report travels in Traffy Fondue, Thailand
items: 1. A resident sees a problem, such as a broken street light or a flooded road.
2. In the LINE messaging app, they send a photo and a short description. The place is added from the phone's location.
3. AI sorts the report by type and sends it to the office that is responsible.
4. People at that office check the report and decide what to do. Some jobs go to a repair team. Bigger ones need money and a plan.
5. The office posts updates. The resident can follow the report and rate the result.

cards.title: Traffy Fondue's growth, as its makers and users report it

events.text: Bangkok's city government starts using it for residents' reports (31 May).
An agreement lets local offices across Thailand use it free for three years (September).
It wins a Thai government award for public service innovation (September). A prize shows that officials valued it, not how many problems were fixed.
Bangkok says it received 588,842 reports in two years and resolved about 79%.
Bangkok's governor tells officials not to close cases with photos that don't show the problem fixed (July).
NSTDA says it is used in all 77 provinces, by more than 34,000 agencies.

sections.heading: A problem on your street
sections.text: In every city, residents notice problems first: a road with a hole in it, a blocked drain, a street light that has stopped working. Fixing them is the job of the city's offices. But a report has to reach the right office, and in a big city there are many. In Thailand, researchers at NECTEC, part of the country's national science agency, NSTDA, built a platform to help. It is called Traffy Fondue. In May 2022, Bangkok's city government began to use it for reports from residents. Since then, many other towns, offices and agencies across Thailand have joined.
sections.simpler: In every city, residents see problems first. A road has a hole. A drain is blocked. A street light stops working. The city's offices must fix them. But a report has to reach the right office. A big city has many offices. In Thailand, researchers at a national science agency built a platform to help. It is called Traffy Fondue. In May 2022, Bangkok's city government began to use it. Many other towns and agencies in Thailand joined later.

sections.heading: What the AI does, and what people do
sections.text: To make a report, a resident uses LINE, a messaging app. They send a photo, a few words and the place. Then AI reads the report and sorts it by type, such as roads, flooding or lights. The system sends it to the office that should deal with it. Sorting and sending is the AI's part of the work. After that, people take over. Officials check the report and decide what to do. Some jobs need only a repair team. A bigger job may need money, a plan and more time. The AI routes the report. People and agencies do the fixing.
sections.simpler: A resident makes a report in LINE, a messaging app. They send a photo, some words and where it is. Then AI reads the report. It sorts it by type, like roads or floods. It sends it to the right office. That is the AI's part. Then people take over. Officials check the report and send workers. A big job needs money and a plan too. So the AI routes the report. People and agencies fix the problem.

sections.heading: What the numbers can and can't show
sections.text: Bangkok says it received 588,842 reports in two years and resolved about 79% of them. These numbers come from the city and the platform's makers, and "resolved" means an official closed the case. In 2025, Bangkok's governor told officials not to close cases with photos that had nothing to do with the problem. So a closed case is not always a fixed problem. In 2025, researchers at Thammasat University in Bangkok studied 98,000 reports and talked with 12 people who knew the system. They found it helped the city see where problems were and plan repairs. They also noted that it needs a smartphone and the internet, which not everyone has.
sections.simpler: Bangkok says it got 588,842 reports in two years. It says about 79% were resolved. These numbers come from the city and the makers. Resolved means an official closed the case. In 2025, the city's leader warned officials about one problem. Some closed cases with photos that did not show the problem. So a closed case is not always a fixed problem. University researchers studied 98,000 reports. It helped the city plan repairs, they found. But it needs a smartphone and the internet.

glossary.definition: A person who lives in a place.
glossary.example: Residents of Bangkok report broken street lights.

glossary.definition: An office or group that does one kind of public work.
glossary.example: NSTDA is Thailand's national science agency.

glossary.definition: To send something along the right path to the right place.
glossary.example: The AI routes each report to the office that should fix it.

glossary.definition: To deal with a problem so that it is finished.
glossary.example: The city says about 79% of reports were resolved.

glossary.definition: A website or app where many people can do the same kind of thing.
glossary.example: Traffy Fondue is a platform for reporting problems.

checks.question: In Traffy Fondue, what does the AI do?

options.text: It fixes the problem by itself
options.feedback: Not quite. Workers fix the problems. Read the second section.

options.text: It sorts each report and sends it on
options.feedback: Yes. The AI sorts the report and sends it to the right office. Then people check it and fix the problem.

options.text: It decides how the city spends money
options.feedback: Not quite. Officials decide what to do and what it costs. Read the second section.

checks.question: Why should you be careful with the number "79% resolved"?

options.text: Some cases were closed but not fixed
options.feedback: Yes. Officials close the cases, and the governor warned that some were closed with photos that didn't show the problem.

options.text: The number was made up by an AI
options.feedback: Not quite. The city reported the number. Read who closes a case in the third section.

options.text: Nobody in Bangkok used the platform
options.feedback: Not quite. Hundreds of thousands of reports were sent. Read the third section.

write.prompt: Explain to a younger student how a report in Traffy Fondue gets from a phone to a repair. Say which steps the AI does and which steps people do.
sentenceStarters: After that, people at the office ...
write.example: First, a resident sees a problem, like a flooded road, and sends a photo and the place in LINE. Then the AI reads the report, sorts it as a flood and sends it to the office that deals with floods. After that, people at the office check it, decide what to do and send workers. If the job is big, they may need money and a plan first. This matters because the AI only gets the report to the right place. The road is fixed by people.

speak.partnerTask: Talk with your partner: a city says it resolved 79 out of every 100 reports. What else would you want to know before you say the platform works well? Each give one question and say why it matters.
speak.independentTask: Say out loud one question you would ask before you trust a number like "79% resolved", and why that question matters.

watch.title: Ethics & AI: Equal Access and Algorithmic Bias
watch.why: People who build and study AI talk about how AI can help everyone, or leave some people out.
watch.beforeQuestion: Who do you think should decide how an AI tool is used in a community?
watch.afterQuestion: Why does it matter who builds an AI tool?
watch.summary: In this video, people who build and study AI talk about fairness. AI tools learn from data, and they are already used in many parts of life. The speakers say AI could help more people get what they need. But AI can also be unfair. If the data, or the people who build a tool, leave some groups out, the tool can work worse for those groups or treat them unfairly. This is called algorithmic bias. The speakers say that people from many different backgrounds should help to build AI. They also say that people must keep checking AI tools, so that the tools help everyone and don't harm the people they leave out.
keyPoints: AI can help more people, or it can treat some people unfairly.
Unfair results often come from data or teams that leave some people out.
People from many backgrounds should help to build and check AI.
watch.contentNote: About 3 minutes 20 seconds. The speakers name the AI companies, car company, universities and groups they work for. The summary was written from DCMP's description of the video and its list of speakers, not from watching it. Preview it first; learners can read the written summary instead.

sources.label: NSTDA (14 September 2022): NSTDA wins Public Sector Excellence Awards (Traffy Fondue, an AI-powered complaint reporting and management system, wins a public service award)

sensitiveNotes: Some learners may live where public services are missing, or where contacting officials is not safe for them. Keep the lesson on Bangkok and on kinds of problems in general. Never ask learners to describe problems where they live in a way that could identify them, or to report anything to any authority.
Don't ask which apps or phones learners or their families have. The point that the platform needs a smartphone and the internet is about access in general, not something to compare between learners.
educatorNotes: What the sources establish (claims/DW10.md). Traffy Fondue was developed by NECTEC, part of Thailand's National Science and Technology Development Agency (NSTDA). Bangkok's city government launched it on 31 May 2022 (Hansen and Dahiya, 2025); residents report through a LINE chatbot with a photo, a description, a category and the place. The researchers describe an AI engine that sorts reports into categories and a workflow that sends each to the responsible agency; NSTDA's 2024 statement adds AI summaries, suggested priorities and filtering of rude language. Repairs are done by the agencies, their teams or contractors; bigger jobs go through evaluation, budgeting and a project. All the scale and speed figures are the city's or the makers' own: Bangkok's 588,842 reports in two years with about 79% resolved (June 2024, from the governor's report, "resolved" not defined); NSTDA's 2026 page (all 77 provinces, 34,786 agencies, over 2 million resolved tickets, average resolution time down from 90 to 15 days). No independent check of repair quality was found. The Thammasat study (98,000 reports, May to December 2022, 12 interviews) reports 84% satisfaction and estimated savings, and notes the platform is digital-first.

Discussion ideas for Speak, with no single right answer: how "resolved" is decided and by whom; how long repairs take; whether some areas or groups send fewer reports (for example people without smartphones); whether repeat reports of the same problem are counted again; what residents say about the results. Lessons 16 and 17 mention Traffy Fondue again briefly.

Revised on 8 November 2026 (Justin's brief of 4 November): removed the “Help or risk?” sort activity, the warm-up, the made-up town of Sunvale (its translation, leaf and eye tools, the evidence, the checks, Write, Speak and Reflect built on them) and SELENA+, so the lesson teaches one documented regional case in depth: Traffy Fondue, Thailand's public reporting platform. The reading covers the problem, the people and institutions (NECTEC and NSTDA, Bangkok's city government), how a report travels, what the AI does (sorts and routes reports) as distinct from what people and agencies do (check, decide, fix), and what the numbers can and can't show (the city's own figures; the governor's 2025 warning about cases closed with unrelated photos; a 2025 Thammasat study). The evidence is real (fictional: false): the steps of a report and a dated timeline. Two factual checks, no think question; Write explains the steps to a younger student; Speak asks what else you'd want to know about a "79% resolved" figure. No fictional case was kept: none added something the real case doesn't. New glossary: resident, agency, route, resolve, platform; new placeholder visual (a report's five steps); sources and claim record replaced.
